A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VITA and retain identifiable matching methods, experiments, and results. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the figures, tables, and equations. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–H are available and readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and real-world manipulation results, inference benchmarks, and ablations in Section 5.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Robomimic evaluations, training curves, and objective and hyperparameter ablations.

M1.justification: The core vision-to-action flow, action autoencoder, and Euler inference procedure remain. Appendix E.1 adds a symmetric InfoNCE objective, and v2 evaluates combining FLD with consistency supervision; Table 6 specifies nonzero consistency and encoder-contrastive weights. FLC itself renames the consistency objective already evaluated in v1 Section 5.4.

E1.justification: v2 adds the Robomimic Square and Can tasks, extending evaluation to single-arm manipulation with seven-dimensional actions. The five simulated AV-ALOHA tasks, PushT, and two real-world AV-ALOHA tasks remain. This expands the represented robotic embodiments and task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains FM, DP, and ACT as comparators. However, the efficiency comparison in Table 3 removes the larger AdaLN FM model and ACT. The remaining FM configurations are matched across naming changes, and Diffusion becoming DDPM does not introduce a new comparator family.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 increases the stated DP and ACT training budgets from 100,000 to 200,000 steps and changes DP inference from 100 to 10 DDPM steps. Table 3 also reports a smaller DP model. These are substantial reported setting revisions, although v2 Table 8 contradicts the 10-step description by specifying inference defaults to 100 timesteps. Actual reruns cannot be established.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's dimensionality and decoding-loss ablations, v2 adds combined FLD/FLC and contrastive-objective comparisons, action and vision VAE ablations, coefficient sweeps, reconstruction-failure examples, and a denoising-process comparison. Appendix B also reports loss-selection and stochasticity investigations. The original dimensionality analysis is largely retained in Appendix B.1 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports best success rates without specifying random-seed aggregation or uncertainty bands. v2 describes Table 1 as means of best validation success rates across three seeds, and Figure 8 explicitly shows means with ±1 standard deviation. This substantially expands statistical reporting, without establishing an increase from any particular earlier run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises VITA/FM success rates on SlotInsertion from 82%/80% to 76%/83% and HookPackage from 82%/72% to 86%/83%, and adds Square and Can results. Table 3 replaces DP's 368.86 ms latency with 2.5985 ms under revised reported settings. Numerous training and ablation curves are added. These are revised or newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting gains. VITA's latency and the real-world outcomes remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 contains flow-matching and loss equations but no corresponding formal guarantees. v2 Section 4.4 and Appendix A add decoder regularity assumptions, an FLD/FLC local-equivalence theorem, a bi-Lipschitz lemma, proofs, and squared-loss and gradient-scaling corollaries. These are substantial theoretical additions, although Appendix A's lower Lipschitz bound does not follow from its stated vector-integral argument.

C1.justification: The central noise-free, conditioning-free, MLP-based policy contributions remain. v2 explicitly promotes prevention of latent-space collapse as an FLD contribution and corrects the quantitative efficiency claim from a 50%–130% latency reduction to a 1.5–2.3× inference speedup, consistent with the retained VITA/FM latency values.

C2.justification: v2 develops the earlier supervision-gap explanation into a latent-collapse account, interprets combined losses as complementary supervision, and explains coherent trajectories decoded from visual latents. It adds interpretations of contrastive alignment, L2 mode-averaging, and stochasticity failures. Its action-VAE discussion is inconsistent: Appendix B retains the comparable-performance claim, while Appendix E.2 and Figures 11–12 report degradation under KL regularization.

D1.justification: Appendices F–H substantially expand reproducibility information with task-specific demonstration counts, image sizes, camera identifiers, state/action definitions, network configurations, loss weights, and baseline optimization settings. Section 5.2 identifies an NVIDIA 4090 for latency measurement. These are mostly newly disclosed details; they do not establish changes to previously unspecified implementations. The project-page link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Robomimic, LeRobot, CLIP, and contrastive predictive coding, and removes the cited text-guided diffusion failure-modes paper. The main positioning against conditioned generative policies and frozen cross-modal latent spaces remains. Much of v1's related-work discussion is retained in Appendix D.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, architecture explanation, and learning-objective narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Main-text related work is condensed while longer discussion appears in Appendix D; dimensionality analysis moves to Appendix B. Terminology is standardized around FLD and FLC, and the method exposition is reorganized around modality mismatch and latent collapse.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, Figure 3 adds Robomimic panels, and the earlier loss-ablation plot is replaced by an expanded comparison. New reconstruction, denoising, learning-curve, and sensitivity figures substantially expand visual presentation. Table 2 is transposed, Table 3 removes rows and its throughput column, and dataset and configuration tables are added.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 provides broader empirical checks, substantially better implementation documentation, seed-based uncertainty reporting, and a corrected efficiency claim. These improve assessment of the core empirical contribution. However, conflicting DP sampling descriptions and action-VAE conclusions weaken clarity, while the new equivalence proof contains an unjustified lower-bound step. The evidence supports a net improvement, tempered by these substantive reporting and theoretical problems.
